claims.claim: Philosophy of religion is the philosophical examination of the themes, concepts, and claims involved in religious traditions, including questions about God or ultimate reality, arguments for and against religious belief, and the epistemic status of faith; it proceeds from no assumed religious standpoint.

Philosophy of religion is distinct from theology, which typically reasons within a faith tradition from its scriptures and authorities, and from the descriptive, historical, and social-scientific study of religion (religious studies).

The cosmological argument is an argument family that infers from facts about the universe (contingency, causation, or its beginning) to a first cause or necessary being; standard objections question the principle that everything needs an explanation and the coherence of a necessary being.

The teleological (design) argument infers a designer from apparent order or purpose in nature, classically via Paley's watch analogy; Hume's Dialogues challenges the analogy, and Darwinian natural selection offers a rival explanation, so the argument remains contested.
Ontological arguments (Anselm, Descartes) derive God's existence from the concept of God alone; the best-known objections are Gaunilo's parody and Kant's claim that existence is not a predicate.

The problem of evil holds that if God is omnipotent, omniscient, and morally perfect, evil's existence appears logically inconsistent with God (logical version, e.g., Mackie) or makes belief in God unreasonable (evidential version, e.g., Rowe); responses include defenses (Plantinga's free will defense) and theodicies (Irenaean soul-making theodicy developed by Hick), all of which remain contested.

Evidentialism holds that belief should be proportioned to evidence — W. K. Clifford called it wrong to believe anything upon insufficient evidence — while fideism (a label attached to thinkers from Tertullian to Kierkegaard) holds that faith is independent of, or opposed to, rational justification.

Religious experiences are experiences that seem to their subjects to be of a religiously significant reality; some philosophers (e.g., Alston) treat them as perception-like grounds for belief, while critics cite cultural shaping and cross-traditional conflict; their evidential status is contested.

Traditional Western theism characterizes God as omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good; these attributes generate puzzles such as the stone paradox, which asks whether an omnipotent being can create a stone too heavy for it to lift and appears to imply a limit either way.

Religious diversity — sincere, informed people holding incompatible religious beliefs — prompts philosophical responses labeled exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism (e.g., John Hick); philosophers present these as positions under evaluation, and the bare fact of diversity does not settle which is correct.

Across the world's traditions, ultimacy is conceptualized differently — as God, Brahman, the Dao, and more — so philosophers increasingly study models of ultimate reality rather than a single shared concept.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do the classical arguments for God's existence succeed?
positions: Defenders hold that cosmological, teleological, and ontological arguments provide good grounds for theistic belief
Critics (e.g., Hume, Kant, and contemporary skeptics) hold that each argument fails at some premise
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents each argument together with its standard objections as contested, attributing views to their proponents and selecting no winner.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the problem of evil a logical contradiction or an evidential challenge?
positions: Logical version (Mackie): evil's existence is inconsistent with an omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good God
Evidential version (Rowe): evil makes theistic belief unreasonable without strict inconsistency
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both formulations and notes that contemporary discussion emphasizes evidential formulations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can the problem of evil be answered?
positions: Free will defense (Plantinga): God and evil are compatible because free creatures choose evil
Soul-making theodicy (Hick): the world exists for moral and spiritual growth
Critics: these responses fail to justify animal suffering and the suffering of young children
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson distinguishes defenses (compatibility only) from theodicies (actual reasons) and presents all as contested.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What is the relation between faith and reason?
positions: Evidentialism (Clifford): belief should be proportioned to evidence
Fideism (Tertullian, Kierkegaard): faith is properly independent of reason
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes both positions, attributes each to its proponents, and endorses neither.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does religious experience provide evidence for religious belief?
positions: Perceptual models (James, Alston): experience can ground belief
Skeptical responses: cultural shaping, conflicting experiences across traditions, and psychological explanation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the evidential status of religious experience as an open, contested question.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How should religious diversity be understood?
positions: Exclusivism: one tradition's core claims are true and incompatible claims false
Inclusivism: one tradition is fully true while others contain genuine partial truth
Pluralism (Hick): traditions are different human responses to one ultimate reality
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the three responses neutrally as positions under evaluation, following the SEP's stated approach of clarifying positions rather than selecting one.

sourceRecords.title: Philosophy of Religion
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the definition of philosophy of religion as the philosophical examination of religious themes and concepts, its scope across worldviews, and its distinct task relative to theology and religious studies.

sourceRecords.title: The Problem of Evil
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the standard formulation (omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect), the logical/evidential distinction, the refutation/defense/theodicy trichotomy, Plantinga's free will defense, and the Irenaean soul-making theodicy associated with Hick, including criticisms.

sourceRecords.title: Cosmological Argument
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the characterization of the cosmological argument as an argument family inferring a first cause, sustaining cause, or necessary being from contingency, causation, or the universe's beginning, with objections to the principle of sufficient reason and the concept of a necessary being.

sourceRecords.title: Teleological Arguments for God's Existence
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the account of design arguments from apparent order and purpose, Hume's Dialogues objections, Darwinian and other rival explanations, and the contested status of fine-tuning and design inferences.

sourceRecords.title: Ontological Arguments
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the account of Anselm's argument from the concept of a being than which no greater can be conceived, Descartes's and Leibniz's versions, Gaunilo's parody, and Kant's objection that existence is not a real predicate.

sourceRecords.title: Omnipotence
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the characterization of omnipotence as maximal power, the stone paradox (a stone so massive the agent cannot move it), and the philosophical search for a consistent analysis of omnipotence.

sourceRecords.title: God and Other Ultimates
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21 (the successor to the retired 'Concepts of God' entry). Supports the claim that ultimacy is conceptualized differently across traditions — God, Brahman, the Dao — and the framing of models of ultimate reality.

sourceRecords.title: Religious Experience
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the characterization of religious experience as experience that seems to its subject to be of religiously significant reality, its distinction from mere feelings, and the contested question of its evidential value (perceptual accounts such as Alston's versus skeptical challenges).

sourceRecords.title: Faith
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the evidentialist principle (proportioning belief to evidence, per Hume) and W. K. Clifford's evidentialism ('wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence'), and the classification of models of faith as evidentialist or fideist.

sourceRecords.title: Fideism
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the definition of fideism as the view that reason is unnecessary or inappropriate for the justification of religious belief, the Tertullian and Kierkegaard associations, and the contrast with the rationalistic tradition of natural theology.

sourceRecords.title: Religious Diversity (Pluralism)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the live HTML entry on 2026-08-21. Supports the pervasiveness of religious diversity, the exclusivism/inclusivism/pluralism taxonomy, John Hick's pluralism, and the SEP's stated aim of clarifying positions rather than supporting a given stance.
